stories.title: PCCP Closes Debt, Equity Funds at Combined $5 Billion
stories.excerpt: PCCP, LLC announced that PCCP Equity X and PCCP Credit XI raised a combined $5 billion in capital commitments across its opportunistic equity and value‑add credit strategies. The two funds mark PCCP’s largest to date. PCCP Equity X, the firm’s opportunistic equity vehicle, closed with $2.7 billion in commitments, an increase from $1.8 billion in Equity IX. PCCP Credit XI, the firm’s value‑add credit vehicle, closed with $2.3 billion, up from $1.7 billion in its predecessor fund. Both funds exceeded their hard cap and focus on U.S. middle‑market investments across the four traditional property sectors: residential for rent, industrial, retail and office. As of September 2026, PCCP has executed about half of the capital raised for Equity X and allocated over one-third of the capital in Credit XI. William Lindsay, co‑founder and senior managing partner with PCCP, said, “What resonated with investors is the fact that we have both a credit business and an equity business, and we have one investment team and one investment committee that services both. They’re very synergistic, so we believe we see a lot more deal flow than most.” The post PCCP Closes Debt, Equity Funds at Combined $5 Billion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PCCP closes $5B across Equity X ($2.7B) and Credit XI ($2.3B), largest funds to date.
Both funds exceed hard caps; half of Equity X and one-third of Credit XI already deployed.
Focus: U.S. middle-market residential, industrial, retail, office with integrated credit-equity strategy.
stories.summary: PCCP, LLC announced the closing of its opportunistic equity fund (Equity X, $2.7B) and value-add credit fund (Credit XI, $2.3B), totaling $5B in capital commitments and exceeding hard caps. Both funds target U.S. middle-market investments across residential, industrial, retail, and office. As of September 2026, PCCP has deployed approximately half of Equity X capital and over one-third of Credit XI, leveraging a unified investment team to capture deal flow across both strategies.
stories.impact: Large capital availability signals sustained appetite for multifamily acquisitions and value-add repositioning across major markets. PCCP's focus on residential middle-market and integrated credit-equity approach indicates strong fundamentals supporting underwriting flexibility; developers should monitor deployment pace and thesis shifts as bellwethers for cap rate and financing availability trends.

stories.title: Adolfson & Peterson Completes Dallas Office to Retail Conversion
stories.excerpt: Adolfson & Peterson Construction (AP) recently completed the shell construction of The Seam, Asana Partners’ 160,000-square-foot upscale shopping and dining destination in Dallas’ Design District. Construction began in March 2025 to renovate the former Oak Lawn Design Plaza at 1444 Oak Lawn Ave. The multi-million-dollar adaptive reuse project repurposed the 1970s-built, nine-acre office park into nearly 50 spaces for retail, restaurants, wellness providers and showrooms, set in an open-air environment.  Morris Adjmi Architects was the design architect, and GFF Design was the architect of record. AP handled all aspects of infrastructure upgrades and shell construction as well as improving the existing buildings by upgrading facades with new exterior insulation finish systems (EIFS). The project also included an MEP overhaul and structural improvements with the addition of new steel and roof work.   The post Adolfson & Peterson Completes Dallas Office to Retail Conversion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 160,000 SF adaptive reuse: Oak Lawn office park (1970s) to retail/dining in Dallas Design District.
Asana Partners conversion adds ~50 retail, restaurant, wellness, showroom spaces in open-air format.
Project complete shell construction March 2025; major MEP, facade, structural upgrades.
stories.summary: Adolfson & Peterson completed shell construction of The Seam, Asana Partners' 160,000-square-foot adaptive reuse project converting the defunct Oak Lawn Design Plaza (nine-acre 1970s office park) into an upscale shopping, dining, and wellness destination in Dallas' Design District. The project included full infrastructure upgrades, MEP overhaul, structural improvements, and facade renovation. Nearly 50 retail, restaurant, wellness, and showroom tenants now occupy the open-air environment.
stories.impact: Signals Dallas Design District's strength and investor confidence in retail/mixed-use adaptive reuse, but more importantly reflects persistent office obsolescence and capital reallocation away from traditional office. Multifamily developers should monitor Design District foot traffic and demographic shifts—repositioned retail/dining often precedes residential densification and can support mixed-use development pipelines nearby.

stories.title: TAWANI Property Management Adding New Amenity Floor to Historic Monroe Building
stories.excerpt: TAWANI Property Management, the community investment arm of TAWANI Enterprises, Inc., is proud to announce that construction is underway on a state-of-the-art amenity floor at the Monroe Building, located at 104 S. Michigan Avenue in Chicago. Expected to open in the fourth quarter of 2026, the space will feature meeting rooms, a boardroom, a conference room, a tenant lounge and flexible open space. Designed by Chicago architect Martin Roche, the 16-story Romanesque-inspired Monroe Building offers a variety of office suites ranging from 295 square feet to 15,455 square feet. “With the addition of the new amenity floor, tenants can take advantage of state-of-the-art technology and flexible gathering spaces for meetings, collaboration, conferences, or simply a change of scenery,” said Kimberley Clark, Property Manager of the Monroe Building. “The space also provides a welcoming destination for tenant employees who work remotely or in hybrid roles and may not need a dedicated office every day, giving them a place to connect, collaborate, and be productive when they come in.” The post TAWANI Property Management Adding New Amenity Floor to Historic Monroe Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: TAWANI adds amenity floor to historic Monroe Building (16-story, 104 S. Michigan, Chicago).
Q4 2026 opening: meeting rooms, boardroom, conference, tenant lounge, flexible space for hybrid workers.
Targets remote/hybrid workforce demand; office repositioning strategy, not multifamily.
stories.summary: TAWANI Property Management is constructing a state-of-the-art amenity floor at the Monroe Building in downtown Chicago, expected to open in Q4 2026. The new floor features meeting rooms, boardroom, conference room, tenant lounge, and flexible gathering spaces designed to serve hybrid and remote workers seeking collaboration environments. The 16-story Romanesque building offers office suites ranging from 295 to 15,455 square feet.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development; this is office repositioning. However, it signals continued office-to-amenity conversion spending in Chicago Loop—suggesting persistent office oversupply and landlord capital deployment away from base building. Developers should monitor Chicago's broader office-to-residential conversion pipeline and whether Loop office weakness accelerates mixed-use residential conversion opportunities.

stories.title: N. Phoenix Apartments Trade for $58.7M
stories.excerpt: Institutional Property Advisors (IPA) brokered the sale of Ascend at Black Canyon, a 260-unit multifamily property in Phoenix, Arizona. The asset traded for $58.7 million, or $225,769 per unit. DR Horton was the seller, Millburn & Company the buyer. Steve Gebing and Cliff David, IPA executive managing director of investments, represented the seller and procured the buyer. IPA’s Gebing added, “North Phoenix is positioned to generate tens of thousands of high-earning jobs supporting the world’s most advanced nanometer chip production for companies such as Apple, Sony, Tesla, and Qualcomm.” Completed on over 10 acres in 2024, Ascend at Black Canyon is a controlled-access community with a resort-style swimming pool, 24-hour fitness center, two dog parks and a pet washing station. The unit mix is one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments with a private patio or balcony. The property is in Phoenix’s Deer Valley urban village close to Interstate 17/Black Canyon Freeway, near the Sonoran Preserve and the Happy Valley Town Center open-air shopping mall. The post N. Phoenix Apartments Trade for $58.7M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: DR Horton sells 260-unit Ascend at Black Canyon (Phoenix) to Millburn & Company for $58.7M ($225.8K/unit).
Property completed 2024; North Phoenix positioned for semiconductor manufacturing job boom (Apple, Sony, Tesla, Qualcomm).
Asset class transaction; broker cites nanometer chip production as major employment tailwind.
stories.summary: Institutional Property Advisors brokered the $58.7 million sale of Ascend at Black Canyon, a 260-unit multifamily property in North Phoenix, from DR Horton to Millburn & Company, at $225,769 per unit. The newly completed (2024) resort-style community is located in Deer Valley urban village near Interstate 17 and Happy Valley Town Center. IPA highlighted North Phoenix's positioning for tens of thousands of high-wage jobs tied to advanced semiconductor nanometer chip production for Apple, Sony, Tesla, and Qualcomm.
stories.impact: North Phoenix multifamily fundamentals strengthening materially: semiconductor manufacturing cluster expansion (likely Intel's Fab expansion, plus supplier/ancillary growth) will drive significant white-collar job and population in-migration to the submarket over 2026–2028. Developers should aggressively acquire land and move projects through entitlement in North Phoenix/Deer Valley and adjacent submarkets before land prices and construction costs rise; window of opportunity to deliver before peak demand is 18–24 months.

stories.title: Greystone Lends $35M on Chicago-Area Apartments Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Isn’t life grand. Multifamily developer Grand Lifestyles has secured $35.4 million of acquisition financing to purchase a multifamily asset in suburban Chicago, Commercial Observer has learned., Greystone closed the Freddie Mac-backed loan to facilitate Grand Lifestyle’s $51.3 million acquisition of The Ponds of Naperville property in Naperville, Ill. from DRA Advisors The financing was originated by Eric Rosenstock, senior managing director at Greystone. “The acquisition market in suburban Illinois is particularly exciting given that it remains one of the few markets experiencing organic rent growth, driven in large part by a lack of new supply and strong underlying multifamily fundamentals,” Rosenstock said in a statement. “The Ponds of Naperville presented Grand Lifestyles with an opportunity to acquire a well-maintained community in an established Chicago-area submarket.” Located at 1331 Modaff Road 30 miles west from Downtown Chicago, the 1988-built property consists of 216 apartments featuring one and two-bedroom units. Community amenities include a clubhouse, recreation room, fitness center, swimming pool, playground, dog park and barbeque area. Grand Lifestyles did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Greystone closes $35.4M Freddie Mac-backed acquisition loan for Grand Lifestyles' $51.3M Naperville purchase.
Property: The Ponds of Naperville (216 units, 1988-built); suburban Chicago 30 miles west of downtown.
Lender cites organic rent growth and lack of new supply in suburban Illinois as market drivers.
stories.summary: Greystone originated a $35.4 million Freddie Mac-backed acquisition loan to facilitate Grand Lifestyles' $51.3 million purchase of The Ponds of Naperville from DRA Advisors. The 216-unit 1988-built property in Naperville, Illinois (30 miles west of downtown Chicago) consists of one- and two-bedroom units with clubhouse amenities. Greystone's originator noted suburban Illinois remains one of few markets experiencing organic rent growth driven by limited new supply and strong fundamentals.
stories.impact: Suburban Chicago (particularly Naperville corridor) exhibiting tight supply-demand dynamics and sustained rent growth—classic early-cycle signal for new development. Developers should prioritize Naperville and similar suburban I-88 corridor locations for new Class A multifamily: financing availability is strong (Freddie Mac execution), existing stock is aging (1988 vintage = 36+ years), and limited new supply supports pricing power. Entry-level rents likely to support 15–20% rent premiums for new construction.

stories.title: Gilbane Building 308 Raleigh Student Housing Units
stories.excerpt: Gilbane Development recently received the green light from the Raleigh City Council to build a 7-story, 308-unit student housing project near North Carolina State University. Site plans show there will be 98 one-bedroom units, 104 two-bedroom units, 32 three-bedroom units and 74 four- and five-bedroom units. The property is 3.61 acres and currently holds the Rhyne’s Gate apartments (shown). The Triangle Business Journal reports that Rhyne’s Gate apartments have 48 affordable housing units that will be replaced with the student housing project. Gilbane Development must provide a 120-day written notice of early lease termination and a one-time relocation assistance payment of $2,500 per unit. A number of NC State student housing projects have been proposed. Peerless Development has proposed a 713-bed development on Crest Road, and RPM Living has plans for a 130-unit student housing project on Horne Street. The post Gilbane Building 308 Raleigh Student Housing Units appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Gilbane Development approved for 308-unit, 7-story student housing near NC State University in Raleigh.
Replacement project: 48 existing affordable units (Rhyne's Gate) demolished; $2,500 relocation assistance per unit required.
Competing pipeline: Peerless 713 beds, RPM Living 130 units also proposed near NC State.
stories.summary: Gilbane Development received Raleigh City Council approval to build a 308-unit, 7-story student housing project on 3.61 acres near North Carolina State University. The project will include 98 one-bedroom, 104 two-bedroom, 32 three-bedroom, and 74 four-/five-bedroom units. It replaces Rhyne's Gate apartments (48 affordable units), with required 120-day lease termination notice and $2,500 per-unit relocation assistance. Additional competing student housing projects (Peerless 713 beds, RPM Living 130 units) are also proposed in the area.
stories.impact: NC State student housing experiencing significant new supply pipeline (1,151 beds across three major projects). Developers should stress-test Raleigh student housing underwriting: competing deliveries will compress occupancy and rent growth. However, if NC State enrollment remains stable or grows and local zoning allows density, the market may absorb supply. Monitor occupancy and rent trends post-Gilbane delivery (likely 2027–2028) before committing to additional student housing starts; Peerless and RPM projects may face lease-up pressure if all three deliver within 12 months.

stories.title: Aquarian Real Estate Partners, 3650 Capital Loan $72M on Chicago-Area Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Rhino Investments Group has secured $72.3 million in financing to acquire Randhurst Village, a 929,899-square-foot. open-air shopping center outside Chicago, Commercial Observer can first report. Rhino acquired the property from DLC Management Corp. for $95 million on Sept. 23 in a sale first reported by The Real Deal. Aquarian Real Estate Partners (AREP) and 3650 Capital provided the acquisition debt, structured as a $45.6 million senior loan from AREP and $26.7 million mezzanine loan from 3650 Capital. Rhino plans a value-add strategy with the debt capital, including leasing vacant spaces and selling outparcel pieces, according to a release. Alpha Capital CRE’s Anthony Longo arranged the financing while Newmark’s Conor Lalor, Keely Polczynski and Brian Schneiderman represented DLC Management on the sale. Jonathan Roth, co-founder and managing partner of 3650 Capital, described Randhurst Village in a statement as “a dominant retail asset with a strong national tenant base,” and noted that the property benefits from strong traffic and has considerable “value-add upside” as an investment due to the affluence of its suburban Chicago market. “Our tremendous confidence in the Rhino team’s ability to execute its business plan is reflected in our existing relationship, and we are delighted to work with AREP on the financing,” added Roth. Located at 1 Randhurst Village Drive in Mount Prospect, a suburb 20 miles west of Downtown Chicago and four miles from O’Hare International Airport, Randhurst Village initially opened in 1962 as a revolutionary retail asset: It was simultaneously the Chicago region’s first enclosed mall and the largest enclosed air-conditioned retail space in the United States. Kevin Holmes, partner and head of AREP, called Randhurst Village “an ideally located property in a strong Chicago submarket.” While it was initially owned by the Randhurst Corporation — a joint venture among now-defunct retailers Carson Pirie Scott, Wieboldt’s and Montg
bullets: Rhino Investment Group secures $72.3M (AREP $45.6M senior + 3650 Capital $26.7M mezz) for Randhurst Village acquisition.
920K SF retail shopping center outside Chicago; $95M total acquisition price from DLC Management.
Value-add: leasing vacant spaces and selling outparcels; retail acquisition, not multifamily.
stories.summary: Rhino Investment Group secured $72.3 million in acquisition financing from Aquarian Real Estate Partners ($45.6M senior) and 3650 Capital ($26.7M mezzanine) to acquire Randhurst Village, a 929,899-square-foot open-air shopping center outside Chicago, purchased from DLC Management for $95 million on September 23. Rhino plans a value-add strategy focusing on leasing vacant spaces and selling outparcel development rights.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily relevance, but signals capital flowing to retail repositioning outside Chicago. Developers should monitor Randhurst's outparcel disposition timeline—shopping centers undergoing value-add often divest land for alternative uses (mixed-use residential, multifamily). If 3650 Capital and AREP execute outparcel sales in suburban Chicago, those pads represent potential multifamily ground-lease or acquisition opportunities; track this deal's progress as a proxy for suburban Chicago land availability.

stories.title: Pistola Denim Takes Nearly 18K SF at ROW DTLA
stories.excerpt: Denim and womenswear company Pistola Denim has signed a 17,922-square-foot office lease at Atlas Capital Group’s ROW DTLA, adding another fashion company to the nearly 2 million-square-foot Downtown Los Angeles complex. Grace Na founded Pistola in 2013. The L.A.-based brand will move its creative team from warehouse and distribution space in Vernon. The terms of the lease were not disclosed. Karen Yi, ROW DTLA’s director of marketing and events, said Pistola joins other fashion brands at the property, which benefits from its proximity to L.A.’s Fashion District. Other office tenants include Adidas, Wilson, Revolve, Fashionphile, HOK, Day One Agency and MidFirst Bank. “Pistola has always been driven by creativity and collaboration, and we wanted a space that could really support that,” Na said in a statement. ROW DTLA spans 32 acres on the edge of the Arts District and includes more than 35 retailers, restaurants, wellness operators and event spaces. It was originally built in the 1920s around the former Los Angeles Terminal Market. But the seven former industrial buildings at the complex were redeveloped and reopened in 2017. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pistola Denim signs 17,922 SF office lease at ROW DTLA (Atlas Capital Group), moving from Vernon warehouse.
ROW DTLA: 2M SF complex, 32 acres, Fashion District proximity; includes Adidas, Revolve, Wilson, other fashion tenants.
Office/creative space leasing, not multifamily; signals DTLA Fashion District clustering.
stories.summary: Pistola Denim, a Los Angeles-based denim and womenswear company founded in 2013, signed a 17,922-square-foot office lease at ROW DTLA, relocating its creative team from warehouse and distribution space in Vernon. The move adds to ROW DTLA's fashion tenant base, which includes Adidas, Revolve, Fashionphile, Wilson, HOK, and others. ROW DTLA spans 32 acres on the edge of the Arts District and includes over 35 retailers, restaurants, wellness operators, and event spaces.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, ROW DTLA's success in anchoring fashion/creative tenants signals Arts District/DTLA south end revitalization and rising commercial/mixed-use demand. Developers should monitor DTLA south and adjacent neighborhoods (Arts District, Little Tokyo) for multifamily absorption trends tied to creative/tech workforce density; residential fill-in developments near ROW DTLA may support higher rents and faster lease-up if fashion/creative employment stabilizes.

stories.title: A Resilient New York City Wins Big at Commercial Observer’s Power Gala
stories.excerpt: The collective might of New York City real estate was on display Tuesday night, when titans of the industry gathered at 7 World Trade Center to celebrate Commercial Observer’s 19th annual Power Gala. The city’s top developers, brokers and investors enjoyed champagne and petite filet mignon canapés against the backdrop of a 40th-floor skyline view — a landscape many of them had a hand in shaping. Attendees take in the view at the Commercial Observer Power Gala at 7 World Trade Center. PHOTO: Greg Morris/for Commercial Observer While power defines the annual soiree, honorees’ tenacity earned this year’s highest praise. Over the past 12 months, New York City’s commercial real estate sector has made significant strides toward recovering its pre-pandemic vigor, including setting new records for office rents and leasing demand despite interest rate hikes and credit concerns. The 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks also loomed large over the event. The significance of the night’s setting and its host, Silverstein Properties, was not lost on anyone. Joseph Meyer, chairman of Observer Media, remembered witnessing the tragic day’s events as a newly hired analyst at Lehman Brothers, and watching the rebirth of Manhattan in its wake. “This market is defined by rapid evolution,” Meyer said. “And it’s really a privilege to stand in front of you, the executives who have done some of the most transformational transactions in the industry.” CO Editor-in-Chief Max Gross noted that one of Commercial Observer’s first galas following the pandemic was held at 7 World Trade Center. “I think most of the people here tonight understand that whatever bad things come our way — and many have, and there will be other bad things in the future — the answer is to roll up our sleeves and get to work,” Gross said. His words kicked off the night’s awards ceremony, which began with Investment Deal of the Year. Mark Mindick, partner and real estate practice leader at Citrin Coope
bullets: Commercial Observer Power Gala highlights NYC CRE resilience; office rents and leasing hit new records.
NYC sector recovering pre-pandemic vigor despite interest rate hikes and credit concerns.
NYC market sentiment and office recovery; limited multifamily-specific data.
stories.summary: Commercial Observer's 19th annual Power Gala celebrated New York City's commercial real estate sector recovery, highlighting new records for office rents and leasing demand over the past 12 months despite interest rate hikes and credit concerns. The event honored industry titans and emphasized the sector's tenacity in recovering pre-pandemic momentum. Silverstein Properties' hosting of the event at 7 World Trade Center underscored NYC's resilience and the role of major developers in shaping the city's landscape.
stories.impact: NYC office recovery signals improving capital formation and investor confidence in high-barrier-to-entry markets. However, multifamily developers should note: strong office-leasing demand may compete for capital and scarce downtown/midtown land, potentially deferring mixed-use residential projects. Monitor NYC multifamily-specific metrics (rents, absorption) separately from office signals; office strength does not guarantee residential tailwinds if remote work persists or if office-to-residential conversion capital is diluted by pure-play office investor activity.

stories.title: South Florida Starchitect Kobi Karp: 5 Questions

His portfolio includes projects such as Four Seasons at the Surf Club in Surfside, 1 Hotel South Beach, Four Seasons Fort Lauderdale, Wynwood 25 and Moxy Wynwood, and he has worked with many of the region’s most prominent developers over the course of his career. And that is pretty phenomenal, because also the rents are traveling between $5 to $6 a foot. And the demand is substantial, and also what people are seeking in those buildings are amenities and functions that create a lifestyle. The people who rent there are in their early 20s to late 30s. The residents get up in the morning and they go to their offices and then come back in the afternoon. There are activities there for the people who live there, and they also bring their friends over. bullets: Kobi Karp (South Florida architect) highlights 635-unit Miami River multifamily with 80% leased in 80 days.
Market thesis: multifamily leading development pipeline in South Florida; Live Local Act incentives discussed.
Operator Flow: strong absorption and rent trajectory signal South Florida residential momentum.
stories.summary: Kobi Karp, founder of Kobi Karp Architecture and Interior Design, discussed South Florida development trends in a Q&A, noting that multifamily apartments are among the most actively financed and moving forward projects. He highlighted a recently completed 635-unit Miami River multifamily property operated by Flow, which achieved 80% occupancy within 80 days of opening and is experiencing strong rent performance. Karp also referenced the Live Local Act as a policy tailwind shaping development strategy in South Florida.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily showing exceptional early-stage lease-up velocity (80% in 80 days) and strong rent growth trajectory. Miami River submarket specifically is attracting capital and achieving strong fundamentals. Developers should prioritize South Florida (Miami, Miami River, Wynwood, Fort Lauderdale) for new multifamily starts: strong underlying demand, operator quality (Flow), and policy support (Live Local Act incentives for workforce housing) create favorable risk-adjusted returns. Monitor Flow's rent trajectory at Miami River completion as a comp for South Florida Class A pricing; early success de-risks similar-profile projects in the pipeline.
